quiz.title: Quick awareness quiz
quiz.intro: Answer one question at a time. You will see a short explanation after you answer.

questions.question: Which situation is an example of cyberbullying?
options: A classmate asks to borrow a pencil.
Someone repeatedly posts hurtful messages about a classmate online.
A friend disagrees with your favorite game.
questions.explanation: Cyberbullying involves harmful behavior using digital tools, such as repeated hurtful messages or posts.

questions.question: You see someone being bullied. What is a safer response?
options: Join in so you fit in.
Forward the post to more people.
Get help from a trusted adult and support the person safely.
questions.explanation: Do not join in or spread harmful content. A trusted adult can help, and you should not put yourself in danger.

questions.question: What should you do if you are unsure whether something is bullying?
options: Ignore all concerns.
Ask a trusted adult for guidance.
Post about the person publicly.
questions.explanation: Context matters. A trusted adult can help you assess the situation and choose a safe next step.

questions.question: Which action can help prevent bullying?
options: Use respectful language and include others.
Laugh when someone is targeted.
Share a hurtful rumor.
questions.explanation: Respect, inclusion, and not spreading rumors help create a safer school community.

questions.question: Who can a student approach to report a concern?
options: Only a random online account.
A trusted adult or the school's approved reporting contact.
No one, ever.
questions.explanation: Students can seek help from a trusted adult, class adviser, Guidance Office, or another verified school contact.

questions.question: Bullying is always just a one-time disagreement between friends.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Bullying usually involves repeated harmful behavior and a power imbalance. A single disagreement is not automatically bullying.

questions.question: You can ask a trusted adult for help even if you are not sure the behavior is bullying.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Trusted adults can help you assess the situation and choose a safe next step, even when you are unsure.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A classmate keeps receiving hurtful comments on her photos. She asks you not to tell anyone. What is the safest response?
options: Keep the secret and do nothing.
Encourage her to talk to a trusted adult, and offer to go with her.
Comment back angrily at the people writing them.
questions.explanation: You can be a good friend without joining the harm. Encourage her to tell a trusted adult and offer support; adults can act while respecting her privacy.

questions.question: SCENARIO: You realize you laughed at a hurtful joke about a classmate yesterday. What is a good next step now?
options: Say nothing. It is over now anyway.
Apologize to the classmate, stop laughing next time, and speak up safely.
Blame the person who told the joke.
questions.explanation: Taking responsibility and changing the behavior helps repair the harm. Laughing along is still joining in, and it is never too late to choose kindness.

activities.title: What would you do?
activities.prompt: You see a hurtful message about a classmate being shared in a group chat. What is a helpful next step?

options.feedback: Sharing or adding to the hurtful content can spread the harm. A safer choice is to avoid forwarding it, support the classmate, and tell a trusted adult.

options.text: Don't share it; support the classmate and tell a trusted adult.
options.feedback: Good choice. Do not forward hurtful content. Support your classmate safely and tell a trusted adult.
Adding to the hurtful content makes the harm worse. A safer choice is to avoid forwarding it, support the classmate, and tell a trusted adult.

activities.title: What would you do?
activities.prompt: At lunch, the same group of classmates always sits together, and one classmate is never invited. What is a helpful next step?

options.text: Ignore it. It is not your business.
options.feedback: Exclusion that keeps hurting someone is a form of bullying. Ignoring it lets the harm continue. A safer step is to include the classmate yourself or tell a trusted adult.

options.text: Invite the classmate to sit with you, or join them if you are also new.
options.feedback: Good choice. Including someone is one of the simplest and strongest ways to prevent bullying.

options.text: Tell the group in front of everyone that they are mean.
options.feedback: Public confrontation can make the situation worse and put you in the middle. A safer step is to include the classmate and tell a trusted adult if it continues.

activities.title: What would you do?
activities.prompt: During recess, you see a classmate being pushed while others laugh. What should you do?

options.text: Record it on your phone to show what happened later.
options.feedback: Recording can spread the harm and embarrass the classmate further. Never share it. Move to safety and get an adult right away.

options.text: Join the group so they do not target you next.
options.feedback: Joining in makes you part of the harm. Safety first: step away and find a teacher or another trusted adult immediately.

options.text: Move to a safe distance and find a teacher or another trusted adult right away.
options.feedback: Good choice. Do not physically intervene if it could put you at risk. Getting an adult quickly is the safest and most helpful action.

activities.title: What would you do?
activities.prompt: A classmate asks you to forward a rumor about another student to the class group chat. What is a safe response?

options.text: Forward it. Everyone is already talking about it anyway.
options.feedback: Forwarding spreads the harm wider, even if you did not start it. Do not pass it on.

options.text: Say no, do not forward it, and tell a trusted adult if it continues.
options.feedback: Good choice. Stopping the chain and telling an adult protects the classmate and keeps you safe.

options.text: Post a public correction and tag the classmate involved.
options.feedback: Public posts about a classmate can add embarrassment and spread the issue further. Say no privately and tell a trusted adult.
